     5  -/
     6  module
     7  
     8  public import Mathlib.Data.Set.Defs
     9  public import Mathlib.Tactic.ToDual
    10  
    11  /-!
    12  # Definitions about upper/lower bounds
    13  
    14  In this file we define:
    15  * `upperBounds`, `lowerBounds` : the set of upper bounds (resp., lower bounds) of a set;
    16  * `BddAbove s`, `BddBelow s` : the set `s` is bounded above (resp., below), i.e., the set of upper
    17    (resp., lower) bounds of `s` is nonempty;
    18  * `IsLeast s a`, `IsGreatest s a` : `a` is a least (resp., greatest) element of `s`;
    19    for a partial order, it is unique if exists;
    20  * `IsLUB s a`, `IsGLB s a` : `a` is a least upper bound (resp., a greatest lower bound)
    21    of `s`; for a partial order, it is unique if exists.
    22  * `IsCofinal s`: for every `a`, there exists a member of `s` greater or equal to it.
    23  * `IsCofinalFor s t` : for all `a ∈ s` there exists `b ∈ t` such that `a ≤ b`
    24  * `IsCoinitial s`: for every `a`, there exists a member of `s` less than or equal to it.
    25  * `IsCoinitialFor s t` : for all `a ∈ s` there exists `b ∈ t` such that `b ≤ a`
    26  -/
    27  
    28  @[expose] public section
    29  
    30  variable {α : Type*} [LE α]
    31  
    32  /-- The set of upper bounds of a set. -/
    33  @[to_dual /-- The set of lower bounds of a set. -/]
    34  def upperBounds (s : Set α) : Set α :=
    35    { x | ∀ ⦃a⦄, a ∈ s → a ≤ x }
    36  
    37  /-- A set is bounded above if there exists an upper bound. -/
    38  @[to_dual /-- A set is bounded below if there exists a lower bound. -/]
    39  def BddAbove (s : Set α) :=
    40    (upperBounds s).Nonempty
    41  
    42  /-- `a` is a least element of a set `s`; for a partial order, it is unique if exists. -/
    43  @[to_dual
    44  /-- `a` is a greatest element of a set `s`; for a partial order, it is unique if exists. -/]
    45  def IsLeast (s : Set α) (a : α) : Prop :=
    46    a ∈ s ∧ a ∈ lowerBounds s
    47  
    48  /-- `a` is a least upper bound of a set `s`; for a partial order, it is unique if exists. -/
    49  @[to_dual
    50  /-- `a` is a greatest lower bound of a set `s`; for a partial order, it is unique if exists. -/]
    51  def IsLUB (s : Set α) : α → Prop :=
    52    IsLeast (upperBounds s)
    53  
    54  /-- A set `s` is said to be cofinal for a set `t` if, for all `a ∈ s` there exists `b ∈ t`
    55  such that `a ≤ b`. -/
    56  @[to_dual /-- A set `s` is said to be coinitial for a set `t` if, for all `a ∈ s` there exists
    57  `b ∈ t` such that `b ≤ a`. -/]
    58  def IsCofinalFor (s t : Set α) := ∀ ⦃a⦄, a ∈ s → ∃ b ∈ t, a ≤ b
    59  
    60  /-- A set is cofinal when for every `x : α` there exists `y ∈ s` with `x ≤ y`. -/
    61  @[to_dual /-- A set is coinitial when for every `x : α` there exists `y ∈ s` with `y ≤ x`. -/]
    62  def IsCofinal (s : Set α) : Prop :=
    63    ∀ x, ∃ y ∈ s, x ≤ y
"}]

[{"type": "text", "text": "# Total variation
In mathematics, the total variation identifies several slightly different concepts, related to the (local or global) structure of the codomain of a function or a measure. For a real-valued continuous function f, defined on an interval [a, b] ⊂ R, its total variation on the interval of definition is a measure of the one-dimensional arclength of the curve with parametric equation x ↦ f(x), for x ∈ [a, b]. Functions whose total variation is finite are called functions of bounded variation.


== Historical note ==
The concept of total variation for functions of one real variable was first introduced by Camille Jordan in the paper (Jordan 1881). He used the new concept in order to prove a convergence theorem for Fourier series of discontinuous periodic functions whose variation is bounded. The extension of the concept to functions of more than one variable however is not simple for various reasons.
